title: P0 hosted API - adaptive batching regression postmortem 2026-07-08
content:
Summary:
On 2026-07-08 at 08:14 UTC we received P0 alerts for elevated request latency and a spike in 5xx errors affecting the hosted API fronting text generation endpoints. Impact lasted ~95 minutes for the largest customers and ~30–45 minutes of degraded performance for most production traffic. The immediate root cause was a faulty change in the adaptive batching heuristic deployed the prior day (runtime PR #1248) that caused aggressive batch-size growth on low-concurrency/erratic-traffic patterns. This in turn induced head-of-line queuing on model workers, causing elevated p50/p95/p99 latencies and eventually request cancellations and 5xx errors for streaming sessions.

Impact (observed):
- Time window: 2026-07-08 08:14 UTC → 09:49 UTC (incident declared resolved at 09:49 UTC)
- Error rate: 5xx rate increased from baseline ~0.2% to peak 7.8% across hosted-api production clusters
- Latency: global generation p50 increased from 120ms to 420ms, p95 from 350ms to 1.9s, p99 from 1.1s to 9.2s at peak
- Streaming: ~18% of active streaming sessions experienced stalled frames or disconnections; customers reported partial transcript dropouts and reconnects
- Affected customers: multiple high-TPS tenants on hosted API; most severe for customers with bursty ingress patterns (bot-like traffic, low concurrency per key)

Detection and escalation:
- 08:14 UTC: internal latency & error-rate SLO alerts fired for hosted-api.prod-global (alert rule: SRE-Gen-High-Err-Latency)
- 08:16 UTC: PagerDuty triggered, on-call SRE (Asha) paged; channel #sre-incident created and initial incident bridge started
- 08:20 UTC: rapid triage identified correlation with recent runtime rollout (canary finished 2026-07-07 22:30 UTC) and an uptick in observed batch-size metrics
- 08:28 UTC: rollback of the adaptive-batching config initiated as an immediate mitigation

Timeline (selected):
- 2026-07-07 22:30 UTC: adaptive batching heuristic v2.3 rolled into production (no canary traffic pattern covering low-concurrency bursts)
- 2026-07-08 08:12 UTC: first weak anomaly noted by telemetry (not auto-alerted because thresholds tuned for steady-state workloads)
- 2026-07-08 08:14 UTC: SRE alerts fired; PD and Slack notification
- 2026-07-08 08:25 UTC: on-call confirmed surge in batch sizes on several worker pools (batch_size metric jumped from median 8→72 in 90s on affected nodes)
- 2026-07-08 08:28 UTC: config rollback command executed (adaptive batching reverted to v2.2 parameters across clusters)
- 2026-07-08 08:45 UTC: p50/p95 latency trends began to improve; 5xx rate reduced but some residual errors persisted
- 2026-07-08 09:10 UTC: additional mitigations: temporary global cap on batch size (max_batch=48), increased worker concurrency and auto-scale headroom for 20 minutes
- 2026-07-08 09:49 UTC: incident declared resolved; monitoring stabilized to baseline

Root cause (concise):
A logic regression in adaptive batching (runtime PR #1248) incorrectly treated brief micro-latency reductions as sustained low-latency signals and increased batch windows aggressively. For traffic patterns with low simultaneous concurrency but frequent short bursts, the heuristic expanded batch sizes, causing long waiting times for first-in requests (head-of-line) while waiting to fill large batches. This behavior magnified GPU queueing and eventually triggered timeouts/back-pressure cascades in the streaming stack causing 5xx and session stalls.

Contributing factors:
- Rollout gaps: the canary run for the heuristic did not include synthetic bursty/low-concurrency traffic profiles (canary targets were steady throughput only)
- Observability blind spot: batch-size growth and batch-wait-ms were not surfaced on the hosting SLO dashboard at an alerting threshold; we relied on downstream latency alerts to detect impact
- Missing circuit breaker: no automatic cap/circuit breaker existed to prevent unbounded batch growth when queueing started to increase latency
- Test coverage: e2e perf tests did not include mixed traffic shape patterns (bursty micro-bursts + idle periods) that would have surfaced the regression
- Runbook omission: runbook lacked explicit rollback command for newer batching config flags (on-call had to assemble rollback steps from runtime runbooks and deploy scripts)

Immediate mitigations applied:
1) Rollback adaptive-batching heuristic to v2.2 parameters (08:28 UTC) — primary fix that arrested batch growth
2) Set emergency global batch cap max_batch=48 (09:10 UTC) to bound worst-case queueing while monitoring
3) Provisioned short-term additional worker headroom and temporarily relaxed autoscaler cooldowns to absorb backlog
4) Tweaked streaming timeouts to be minimally more tolerant while rollback took effect (short-lived change)

Longer-term remediation (owners and due dates):
- Add traffic-shape canary harness and include bursty/low-concurrency synthetic profiles (owner: Miguel Santos, due: 2026-07-22)
- Expose batch-size and batch-wait-ms metrics on hosted-api SLO dashboard and add alerting (owner: Evelyn Cho, due: 2026-07-15)
- Implement adaptive-batching safety caps and an automatic latency-based circuit breaker (owner: Jordan Lee, due: 2026-08-05)
- Expand e2e perf tests to include mixed traffic shapes; add regression test for PRs modifying batching heuristic (owner: Ravi Menon, due: 2026-07-29)
- Update on-call runbook: explicit rollback commands, quick cap toggles, and checklist for streaming session recovery (owner: Asha Patel, due: 2026-07-12)
- Post-deploy monitoring playbook: run 30m synthetic burst tests after any batching heuristic change before marking rollout complete (owner: eng-release, due: 2026-07-20)

Follow-ups and verification plan:
- Weekly telemetry audit for 6 weeks to verify batch-size distribution and latency correlation across clusters (owner: telemetry team, report: 2026-08-19)
- Targeted canary rollout for v2.3 with new canary harness; require 24h green on mixed-shape traffic before global rollout (owner: release-engineering)
- Retrospective with product/serving-runtime to discuss design trade-offs for aggressive batching vs user-facing latency (schedule: 2026-07-14)

Runbook delta (what we changed to make response faster):
- Added single-button rollback for batching flags to release console (released 2026-07-09)
- Added emergency cap toggle in ops console (released 2026-07-09)
- Documented exact telemetry panels and query names to check in first 5 minutes of an incident (committed 2026-07-09)

Lessons learned (concise):
- Batching heuristics can improve throughput but are brittle for non-steady traffic; canary scenarios must represent the full spectrum of real customer traffic shapes.
- Observability must include higher-fidelity indicators of internal batching/waiting behavior to detect problems before customer-facing SLOs degrade.
- Small rollout gaps (missing synthetic scenarios) are high risk for infra changes that change request scheduling behavior.

Appendix: useful commands and quick references
- rollback batching flags (ops): ./deploy_ctl rollback-config --namespace=hosting --config adaptive-batching --to=v2.2
- emergency cap toggle (ops console): Settings → Compute → Adaptive batching → set max_batch=48 → apply
- tracing queries: traces.service:hosted-api | filter batch_size>32 | group_by node, sum(duration_ms)
- related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1248

Postmortem owner sign-off:
- Asha Patel (SRE on-call lead) — signed 2026-07-10
- Miguel Santos (runtime) — acknowledged 2026-07-10

Notes to self / informal after-action comments:
- On-call felt confused initially because the p50/p95 spike pattern looked like a model perf regression; batch-size metrics saved the diagnosis. Make these metrics 'first-class' for future paging rules.
- Consider an automatic canary rollback if batch_size growth rate exceeds X per minute during rollout
